decisions.mark: concludes that this enforces API opacity at COMPILE time by breaking the member name, rather than by hiding the struct layout — the fields remain visible and sized
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "By default each field is really named `private_state`, `private_flags`, and so on. Code that writes `ssl->state` against the public header fails to compile, so the field is effectively private." | WHY: The answer explains that opacity is enforced at compile time by renaming members via `private_##member`, so the fields stay in the struct and only their names are broken. Code that writes `ssl->state` against the public header fails to compile, so the field is effectively private. | WHY: The answer says opacity is enforced at compile time by renaming members to `private_*`, so the fields stay in the struct and only the name breaks. It never says the layout is hidden. || QUOTE: By default each field is really named `private_state`, `private_flags`, and so on. Code that writes `ssl->state` against the public header fails to compile, so the field is effectively private. | WHY: The answer says opacity is enforced at compile time by renaming members to `private_*` through name mangling, so access by the original name fails.
